title: Genuine multimodality in Hidden Markov Models and Parallel Tempering
text:
In the previous notebook we explored the Bayesian approach to hidden Markov models, highlighting that the likelihood is invariant under permutations of the state labels and that, under exchangeable priors, this invariance is transfered to the posterior density. As a consequence, each mode of the posterior of an \(m\)-state HMM appears in \(m!\) symmetric copies, one for each permutation of the labels. This makes state-specific posterior summaries, such as the posterior mean of each state’s parameters, meaningless unless the labels are fixed in some way. We discussed several methods to deal with this label switching problem, namely ordering constraints, post-hoc relabeling and label-invariant quantities.
In this notebook we explore a scenario in which, even after accounting for label switching, the posterior density has several modes that are not relabelings of one another, a situation known as genuine multimodality (Grün and Leisch 2009). Since the methods discussed in the previous notebook assume that every mode is a permuted copy of a single one, they cannot resolve this problem. Genuine multimodality also exposes the limitations of general-purpose MCMC methods, such as the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler used by Stan, whose chains tend to remain in the mode where they started. An incomplete exploration of the posterior yields summaries that describe only part of it, missing some modes and misrepresenting the relative weight of the others, so the consequences of this problem are not only computational but also inferential (Gallegos-Herrada, Leos-Barajas, and Rosenthal 2026).
Parallel tempering, the class of MCMC methods on which this series focuses, is designed for posterior densities with several modes separated by regions of low probability. Before introducing it, we need to understand when genuine multimodality arises in HMMs and why general-purpose samplers fail to handle it. In later notebooks we apply these ideas to HMMs and to a more general class of models, the Markov switching models.
The rest of this notebook is organized as follows. In Section 2 we define genuine multimodality and describe situations in which it may arise in practice. In Section 3 we use simulated data to show how Stan fails to explore the full posterior density in the presence of genuine multimodality. Finally, in Section 4 we introduce parallel tempering, a class of MCMC algorithms that runs several chains on tempered versions of the posterior and exchanges states between them, which allows the sampler to move between modes separated by regions of low probability.

title: Genuine multimodality in Hidden Markov Models and Parallel Tempering
text:
2.1 Relabeling the states
Let \(S_m\) denote the set of the \(m!\) permutations of the labels \(\{1, \dots, m\}\). Each permutation \(\nu \in S_m\) is a one-to-one function that assigns a new label \(\nu(j)\) to each label \(j\). With a slight abuse of notation, we write \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) for the parameter vector obtained by relabeling the states according to \(\nu\). Its components are
\[
\gamma'_{ij} = \gamma_{\nu(i)\nu(j)}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}'_j = \boldsymbol{\eta}_{\nu(j)}, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, m.
\tag{1}\]
The same permutation is applied simultaneously to the state-dependent parameters and to both the rows and the columns of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\). Permuting only some components, for instance swapping \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_2\) while keeping \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) unchanged, produces in general a different model. Since \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is the stationary distribution of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), it is relabeled in the same way, \(\delta'_i = \delta_{\nu(i)}\).






NoteExample



Consider a 3-state HMM with normal emissions, state means \((\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3) = (-2, 0, 3)\) and transition probability matrix
\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma} =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.80 & 0.10 & 0.10 \\
0.20 & 0.70 & 0.10 \\
0.05 & 0.15 & 0.80
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Take the permutation that swaps states 1 and 3, so \(\nu(1) = 3\), \(\nu(2) = 2\) and \(\nu(3) = 1\). Applying Equation 1 gives \((\mu'_1, \mu'_2, \mu'_3) = (3, 0, -2)\) and
\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}' =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.80 & 0.15 & 0.05 \\
0.10 & 0.70 & 0.20 \\
0.10 & 0.10 & 0.80
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both parameter vectors describe exactly the same model. The state with mean \(3\) is now called state 1, and its row and column in \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}'\) moved accordingly.

title: Genuine multimodality in Hidden Markov Models and Parallel Tempering
text:
2.2 Invariance and equivalence classes
As we seen in the previous notebook, relabeling the states does not change the distribution of the observations, so the likelihood is invariant under any permutation of the labels,
\[
L(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})) = L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \quad \text{for all } \nu \in S_m.
\]
If, in addition, the prior is exchangeable, that is, \(p(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) for all \(\nu \in S_m\), the posterior density inherits the same invariance,
\[
p(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) \quad \text{for all } \nu \in S_m.
\]
This invariance can be described through equivalence classes on \(\Theta\). Following Gallegos-Herrada, Leos-Barajas, and Rosenthal (2026) and Grün and Leisch (2009), we say that two parameter vectors \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1, \boldsymbol{\theta}_2 \in \Theta\) are equivalent if one is a relabeling of the other,
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta}_1 \sim \boldsymbol{\theta}_2 \iff \exists\, \nu \in S_m \text{ such that } \boldsymbol{\theta}_1 = \nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2).
\]
In the example above, the two parameter vectors are equivalent. This relation is an equivalence relation, since every vector is a relabeling of itself (identity permutation), relabelings can be undone (inverse permutation), and two successive relabelings are again a relabeling (composition of permutations). As any equivalence relation, it partitions \(\Theta\) into disjoint equivalence classes, each containing all relabelings of a given parameter vector. Both the likelihood and the posterior are constant within each class, so each class represents a single model and its elements differ only in the names given to the states.
A class contains at most \(m!\) elements. It contains exactly \(m!\) elements when all the \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_j\) are different, because then every permutation other than the identity moves at least one \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_j\) and produces a different point of \(\Theta\). If two states had exactly the same parameters, swapping them would leave \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) unchanged and the class would be smaller.

text:
2.3 Modes of the posterior
A point \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^* \in \Theta\) is a mode of the posterior if it is a local maximum, that is, if there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*\) such that \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}^* \mid \mathbf{y}) \geq p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in U\). We denote by \(\mathcal{M}\) the set of all modes of the posterior. The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the highest of them, but \(\mathcal{M}\) also contains every local maximum. Following Grün and Leisch (2009), if the posterior is constant on a peak, the whole peak counts as a single mode.
Because the posterior is invariant, if \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*\) is a mode then every relabeling \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*)\) is also a mode with the same posterior density. Hence \(\mathcal{M}\) is made of complete equivalence classes. When all the \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_j\) are different and the modes are isolated points, each class in \(\mathcal{M}\) contributes exactly \(m!\) symmetric modes. In particular, the MAP is not unique, since \(m!\) different points of \(\Theta\) share the maximum value of the posterior.






NoteExample



In the 3-state example, if the posterior has a mode with means \((-2, 0, 3)\), it also has modes with means \((-2, 3, 0)\), \((0, -2, 3)\), \((0, 3, -2)\), \((3, -2, 0)\) and \((3, 0, -2)\), each with its transition probability matrix relabeled accordingly. These six modes are different points of \(\Theta\) with the same posterior density, and they all belong to the same equivalence class.


These statements assume that the posterior has at least one mode, which requires it to be bounded. With normal emissions, a prior on the standard deviations is needed for this, since otherwise the likelihood can grow without bound when a standard deviation shrinks to zero.

text:
2.4 Genuine multimodality
The symmetric modes described above are the label switching problem of the previous notebook. They all belong to the same class and therefore describe the same model. Genuine multimodality refers to modes that belong to different classes.

Definition 1 (Genuine multimodality) The posterior density is genuinely multimodal if there exist two modes \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1, \boldsymbol{\theta}_2 \in \mathcal{M}\) such that
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta}_1 \neq \nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2) \quad \text{for all } \nu \in S_m,
\]
that is, if \(\mathcal{M}\) contains modes from at least two different equivalence classes.

An equivalent way to state this definition uses a restricted parameter space \(\tilde{\Theta} \subset \Theta\) that contains exactly one representative of each equivalence class, for instance the vectors that satisfy an ordering constraint on the state means. The posterior is not genuinely multimodal if, restricted to \(\tilde{\Theta}\), it has a single mode, and it is genuinely multimodal if it has several.
This formulation shows why the methods of the previous notebook are not enough. An ordering constraint keeps one copy of each class, so if \(\mathcal{M}\) contains several classes, several modes remain after imposing it. Post-hoc relabeling algorithms face a similar problem, since they assume that all the modes are relabelings of a single one. Moreover, genuine modes can have different heights and lead to different interpretations of the states, so posterior summaries computed over draws from several genuine modes mix different models.

section: 2.5 When does genuine multimodality arise in HMMs?
text:
2.5 When does genuine multimodality arise in HMMs?
Grün and Leisch (2009) show that genuine multimodality occurs in finite mixture models when different parameterizations induce similar mixture distributions. An HMM whose transition probability matrix has identical rows is a finite mixture, so these results apply to HMMs as a special case. In general, however, the dependence between observations carries additional information about the states, and it is not obvious whether the same phenomenon persists.
Genuine multimodality in HMMs can arise from two broad sources. The first is uncertainty in the specification of the model. Fitting a number of states different from the one that generated the data is a typical example. With too few states, the model can merge the true states in several different ways, and with too many, it can split them in several different ways. In both cases each arrangement may correspond to a different mode of the posterior. A related situation occurs when some state-dependent distributions are nearly indistinguishable. Even if the number of states is correct, the data provide little information to decide which state explains which observations, and the likelihood may compensate through different values of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\).
The second source is a limited amount of data, which can produce genuine multimodality even when the model is correctly specified. With few observations, the likelihood is not informative enough to concentrate the posterior around a single equivalence class. In HMMs, the relevant amount of information depends not only on the length of the series but also on how many transitions between states it contains, since a series with very persistent states provides few switches from which to learn \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\). Under correct specification, we expect these additional modes to vanish as the number of observations grows, while those caused by misspecification may persist.
In this notebook we illustrate both sources with simulated data. In the first example the model is misspecified, since we fit an HMM with fewer states than the one that generated the data. In the second example the model is correctly specified, but the series is short, so the data contain little information about the parameters. For this second example we also fit the same model to a longer series, which serves as a reference in which we expect the additional modes to disappear. In Section 3 we verify empirically whether each setting produces genuine multimodality and how Stan behaves in its presence.

3.1 Example 1. A misspecified model
Grün and Leisch (2009) describe the fitting of finite mixture models as an ill-defined estimation problem, since completely different parameterizations can induce similar mixture distributions. As discussed in Section 2, the same difficulty extends to HMMs. Misspecification makes it more severe. When the fitted model has fewer states than the one that generated the data, no parameter vector reproduces the true distribution of the observations, and several different ways of merging the true states may approximate it almost equally well. Each of these approximations may correspond to a different mode of the posterior.
To illustrate this, we simulate a 3-state HMM with normal state-dependent distributions, unit variances and well-separated means located at \(-4\), \(0\) and \(4\). The transition probability matrix is chosen so that it is unchanged when states 1 and 3 are swapped. Together with the symmetric means, this design makes the competing ways of merging the true states equally plausible in expectation. In any particular sample, however, the states are not visited in exactly the same proportions, and as we show below, even small differences produce modes with very different posterior mass. We use a relatively long series of \(T = 1000\) observations, since modes caused by misspecification are not expected to disappear as more data become available. The complete design is summarized in Table 1.

The next step is to specify a Stan model for an HMM with only two states. As in the previous notebook, we impose an ordering constraint on the state means, \(\mu_1 < \mu_2\), so that label switching is removed and any multimodality that remains in the posterior is genuine. All priors are proper, which will also be required when we fit the same model with parallel tempering. We use \(\mu_j \sim N(0, 5^2)\) for the state means, a \(\text{Gamma}(2, 0.5)\) prior with shape \(2\) and rate \(0.5\) for the standard deviations, and a \(\text{Dirichlet}(1, 1)\) prior for each row of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\). The prior on \(\sigma_j\) deserves a comment. A half-normal prior, a common default, has its maximum density at \(\sigma_j = 0\) and does not prevent a state from collapsing onto a single observation, where the likelihood grows without bound. The Gamma prior with shape \(2\) vanishes at zero and keeps the posterior bounded. The scales of these priors are chosen to cover not only the parameters of the data-generating process but also those of the misspecified fit. For instance, a state that merges two true states with means \(-4\) and \(0\) has a standard deviation close to \(\sqrt{1 + 2^2} \approx 2.2\), close to the mode of this prior. The Stan code for the model is presented below.


stan/03_hmm_misspec_ex1.stan

// data
data {
  int<lower=1> T;   // number of observations
  int<lower=1> m;   // number of states
  array[T] real y;  // observations
}

// parameters
parameters {
  ordered[m] mu;                  // means of the state-dependent distributions
  array[m] real<lower=0> sigma;   // standard deviations of the state-dependent distributions
  array[m] simplex[m] gamma;      // rows of Gamma, gamma[i] is the i-th row
}

// transformed parameters
transformed parameters {
  matrix[m, m] Gamma;
  row_vector[m] delta;

  for (i in 1:m) {
    Gamma[i] = gamma[i]';
  }
  delta = rep_row_vector(1, m) / (identity_matrix(m) - Gamma + rep_matrix(1, m, m));
}

// model
model {
  matrix[m, T] log_omega;  // log densities of each observation under each state

  // Priors
  mu ~ normal(0, 5);
  sigma ~ gamma(2, 0.5);  // shape 2 and rate 0.5, vanishes at zero
  for (i in 1:m) {
    gamma[i] ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1, m));
  }

  // State-dependent log densities
  for (t in 1:T) {
    for (j in 1:m) {
      log_omega[j, t] = normal_lpdf(y[t] | mu[j], sigma[j]);
    }
  }

  // Likelihood through the forward algorithm
  target += hmm_marginal(log_omega, Gamma, delta');
}

Before sampling from the posterior defined in 03_hmm_misspec_ex1.stan, we characterize it by searching for its modes. Optimization is cheaper than sampling and, from a given initial value, it climbs to the nearest local maximum of the posterior density. By running the optimizer from many dispersed initial values, we obtain a map of the modes, their heights and how often each one is reached. The modes are a property of the posterior and do not depend on where the optimizer starts, but the mode it reaches does. If all runs end at the same point, this is evidence, although not a proof, that the posterior has a single mode, since a finite number of runs can always miss one. This map will later serve as a reference to judge whether the Stan chains explore the whole posterior.
We generate initial values for all the parameters with prior distributions and then we use the Optimize module of Stan. We run \(50\) optimizations and

from cmdstanpy import CmdStanModel
import logging
import pandas as pd
logging.getLogger("cmdstanpy").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

# Load and prepare the data
df_stan = pd.read_csv("../data/03_hmm_3state_ex1.csv")

stan_data = {
    "T": df_stan.shape[0],
    "m": 2, # Here we specify fewer states
    "y": df_stan["y"].to_numpy(),
}

# Compile the Stan program
model = CmdStanModel(stan_file="../stan/03_hmm_misspec_ex1.stan")

# Generate random numbers for reproducibility
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)

# Optimization using different starting values
df_opts = []
for i in range(50):
    
    init = {
        "mu": np.sort(rng.uniform(-7, 7, size=2)),
        "sigma": rng.uniform(0.5, 4, size=2),
        "gamma": rng.dirichlet(np.ones(2), size=2),
    }
    
    fit_opt = model.optimize(data=stan_data, seed=0, inits=init)
    df = fit_opt.optimized_params_pd
    df_opts.append(df)

# DF with the optimized parameters
df_concat = pd.concat(df_opts).reset_index(drop=True)

# We show results for the emissions

df_table["lp__"] = df_table["lp__"].round(1)

# Summaries of the optimization

title: Introduction to Hidden Markov Models
text:
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a special type of state-space model in which the observed process depends on an underlying, unobserved (hidden) Markov chain. They were introduced in the late 1960s by Leonard Baum and colleagues at the Institute for Defense Analyses, originally under the name “probabilistic functions of Markov chains” — the term “Hidden Markov Model” came later. The framework stayed largely within engineering circles until the 1980s, when researchers at Bell Labs, most notably Lawrence Rabiner, built on it to create the first practical speech recognition systems; Rabiner’s widely cited 1989 tutorial is what carried HMMs well beyond speech processing. Since then they have become a standard tool in bioinformatics, finance, ecology, and the social sciences, wherever a sequence of observations is thought to arise from an unobserved process switching between a small number of discrete states.

text:
Likelihood

For observed data \(y_1, ..., y_T\), we want to compute the likelihood \(L_T\) — the probability of these particular observations arising from an \(m\)-state HMM with initial distribution \(\delta\) and transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\).
To express \(L_T\) compactly, for each observation \(y_t\) we define an associated \(m \times m\) diagonal matrix whose \(i\text{-th}\) entry is the density (or probability) of \(y_t\) under state \(i = 1, ..., m\):
\[\mathbf{P}(y_t) = \text{diag}\big(p_1(y_t), p_2(y_t), \dots, p_m(y_t)\big)\]
Assuming that the Markov process is homogeneous and \(\delta\) is the stationary distribution, we can demonstrate that the likelihood is given by
\[L_{T} = \boldsymbol{\delta P}(y_1)\boldsymbol{\Gamma P}(y_2)\dots\boldsymbol{\Gamma P}(y_t)\boldsymbol{1}'\]

Forward algorithm
Given known values of \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) (and the state-dependent distributions), we can compute the likelihood recursively — an approach known as the “forward algorithm”. This algorithm is useful because it allows us to avoid computing all \(m^{T}\) possible trajectories.
First, we define \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t\) as the partial matrix product of the likelihood up to time \(t\),
\[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(y_1)\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_2)\dots\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_t)\]
With this convention, we have for time \(1\),
\[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(y_1)\]
and, for \(t = 2, \dots, T\), the recursive relationship
\[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{t-1}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_t)\]
Finally, the likelihood is recovered by summing over the \(m\) possible states at time \(T\),
\[L_T = \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{T}\mathbf{1}'\]
Rather than expanding the full matrix product at once, the forward algorithm updates a single \(1 \times m\) vector \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t\) at each point in time. This reduces the computational cost of evaluating the likelihood from \(O(m^T)\) to \(O(Tm^2)\).

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

np.random.seed(0)

# Transition probability matrix
Gamma = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.3, 0.7]])

m = 2
states = np.arange(m)

# Stationary distribution
A = np.vstack([(Gamma.T - np.eye(m))[:-1], np.ones(m)])
b = np.zeros(m); b[-1] = 1
delta = np.linalg.solve(A, b)

# Observation process parameters
mu = np.array([0, 2])
sigma = np.array([1, 1])

# Simulate data
T = 20
C = np.zeros(T, dtype=int)
Y = np.zeros(T)

C[0] = np.random.choice(states, p=delta)
Y[0] = np.random.normal(loc=mu[C[0]], scale=sigma[C[0]])

for t in range(1, T):
    C[t] = np.random.choice(states, p=Gamma[C[t-1]])
    Y[t] = np.random.normal(loc=mu[C[t]], scale=sigma[C[t]])

# Forward algorithm
P1 = np.diag(norm.pdf(Y[0], loc=mu, scale=sigma))
alpha = delta @ P1

for t in range(1, T):
    Pt = np.diag(norm.pdf(Y[t], loc=mu, scale=sigma))
    alpha = alpha @ Gamma @ Pt

L_T = alpha.sum()
L_T

Maximization of the likelihood
In the previous code snippet, the likelihood came out to be practically zero. (Zucchini, MacDonald, and Langrock 2016) explains that this happens because the likelihood is a product of matrices so the elements of \(L_T\) tend to zero as \(t\) grows larger for discrete state-dependent distributions, or possibly to infinity for continuous ones — exhibiting underflow or overflow, respectively. Moreover, since we are dealing with matrices rather than scalars, we cannot simply compute the log-likelihood as the sum of the logs of its factors.
To overcome this, we can scale the likelihood by scaling \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\). To illustrate this, consider a stationary and homogeneous m-state HMM and define for \(t=0, 1, ..., T\) the vector
\[\boldsymbol{\phi}_t = \boldsymbol{\alpha}_t / w_t, \quad \text{where } w_t = \boldsymbol{\alpha}_t\mathbf{1}'\]
with \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_0 = \boldsymbol{\delta}\) and \(w_0 = 1\). Since \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_t\) is normalized to sum to 1, \(w_t\) can be recovered recursively as
\[w_t = w_{t-1}\big(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{t-1}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_t)\mathbf{1}'\big)\]
Because \(L_T = w_T\), the log-likelihood is now a sum of scalars instead of a product of matrices,
\[\log L_T = \sum_{t=1}^{T}\log(w_t/w_{t-1})\]
At each step, we normalize \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t\) to obtain \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_t\), and accumulate the scaling factor \(w_t\) on the log scale — avoiding underflow entirely.

In addition to underflow or overflow when computing the likelihood, computational problems can also arise when maximizing it — namely, slow convergence under constrained optimization, and the presence of multiple maxima in the likelihood surface.
Parameter constraints appear, for example, in \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), since each row must sum to \(1\) and every entry must be non-negative; they can also appear in the parameters of the state-dependent distributions (e.g., when a parameter can only take positive values). To avoid implementing these constraints directly, we can make use of reparametrization.
For the state-dependent distributions, the nature of the restriction indicates what kind of reparametrization we can use. For example, if the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are positive, we can define \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\log} = \log(\boldsymbol{\theta})\), maximize the likelihood with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\log}\) to obtain \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\log}\), and then recover the original parameters by transforming back with \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\log})\). Similarly, when the parameters take values in the interval \((0,1)\), we can make use of the logit function instead.
The transition probability matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) requires a different treatment, since its constraint is not on individual entries but on entire rows: although \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) has \(m^2\) entries, it has only \(m(m-1)\) free parameters, because each row must sum to \(1\). We call the unconstrained parameters \(\tau_{ij}\) (for \(i \neq j\)) the working parameters, and the entries \(\gamma_{ij}\) of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) the natural parameters — the same terminology applies to \(\log(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) versus \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) in the previous case.
To go from working to natural parameters, define \[\nu_{ij} = \begin{cases} \exp(\tau_{ij}) & i \neq j \\ 1 & i = j \end{cases}\]
and normalize each row so it sums to \(1\), \[\gamma_{ij} = \nu_{ij} \Big/ \sum_{k=1}^{m}\nu_{ik}\]
Since every \(\nu_{ij} > 0\), this normalization guarantees \(\gamma_{ij} \in (0,1)\) and \(\sum_j \gamma_{ij} = 1\) automatically — the t.p.m. constraints are satisfied by construction, without ever having to impose them explicitly during optimization. Explicitly, for \(i \neq j\), \[\gamma_{ij} = \frac{\exp(\tau_{ij})}{1 + \sum_{k \neq i}\exp(\tau_{ik})}\]
To go in the opposite direction — recovering working parameters from an already-known \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) — we invert the transformation, \[\tau_{ij} = \log(\gamma_{ij}/\gamma_{ii}), \quad i \neq j\]
As before, estimation proceeds in two steps: (1) maximize \(L_T\) with respect to the unconstrained working parameters — \(\{\tau_{ij}\}\), together with any other reparametrized parameters such as \(\log\sigma_i\) — and (2) transform the resulting estimates back to the natural parameters \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}\).

Maximization of the likelihood using the Baum-Welch algorithm
One of the most used algorithms for the MLE of the parameters of an HMM when the Markov process is homogeneous but not necessary stationary is the Baum-Welch algorithm wich is a special case of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm.
The algorithm makes use of the forward probabilities \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{t}\) wich are
\[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(y_1)\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_2)\dots\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_t)\]
and also the backward probabilities \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{t}\)
\[\boldsymbol{\beta}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_{t+1})\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_{t+2})\dots\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{P}(y_{T})\bold{1}'\]
Noting that the sequence of states of the Markov process of an HMM is not observed, we can treat those states as missing data and therefore use te EM algorithm, an algorithm useful in situations like this one.
An informal way to describe the EM algorithm is that you start by choosing starting values of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) and then repeat the E-step and M-step until some converfence criterion is reached:

E-step: compute the conditional expectations of the missing data given the observations and current estimate of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\).
E-step: Mazimize, with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). with the functions of the missing data repaced in it by their conditional expectations

One disadvantage is that convergence is guaranteed locally.
In the context of HMM, we represent the sequence of states \(c_1, c_2, ..., c_t\) as zero-one random variables as follows:
\[u_{j}=1 \text{ if and only if }c_{t}=j \text{ } (t = 1,...,T)\]
and
\[v_{jk}(t)= 1 \text{ if and only if }c_{t}=j \text{ } (t = 2,...,T)\]
With this, the log-likelihood of the observations \(y_1,...,y{T}\) and the missing data \(c_1,...,c{T}\);
\[
\log\big(\Pr(y_1,\ldots,y_T,c_1,\ldots,c_T)\big) = \log\left(\delta_{c_1}\prod_{t=2}^{T}\gamma_{c_{t-1}c_t}\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{c_t}(y_t)\right)
\]
Using \(v_{jk}(t)\) and \(u_{j}=1\), the complete data loglikelihood is
\[
\log\big(\Pr(\mathbf{x}^{(T)}, \mathbf{c}^{(T)})\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} u_j(1)\log\delta_j + \sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\left(\sum_{t=2}^{T} v_{jk}(t)\right)\log\gamma_{jk} + \sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{t=1}^{T} u_j(t)\log p_j(x_t)
\]
and we can use this equation to estimate the parameters using the EM algorithm as follows:

E-step Estimate the conditional expectations \(\hat{u}_{j}(t)\) and \(\hat{v}_{jk}(t)\):

\[\hat{u}_{j}(t) = \text{Pr}(C_{t} = j| y_1,...,y_{t}) = \frac{\alpha_{t}(j)\beta_{t}(j)}{L_t}\]
and
\[\hat{v}_{jk}(t) = \text{Pr}(C_{t-1} = j, C_{t} = k | y_1,...,y_{t}) = \frac{\alpha_{t}(j)\beta_{t}(j)}{L_t}\]
This quantities are used to replace the values \(\hat{u}_{j}(t)\) and \(\hat{v}_{jk}(t)\) in the log-likelihood formula.

M-step Once replaced the values \(\hat{u}_{j}(t)\) and \(\hat{v}_{jk}(t)\) by \(\hat{u}_{j}(t)\) and \(\hat{v}_{jk}(t)\), respectively, we maximize the CDLL with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\), \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) and \(\bold{p}(y)\). We note that the CDLL is a sum of three terms that do not share common terms so the maximization problem consist in maximizing three independent sums.

\(\sum_{j=1}^m\hat{u}_{j}(t)\text{ log}(\delta_{j})\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\);
\(\sum_{j=1}^{m} \sum_{k=1}^{m}\big(\sum_{t=2}^{T}\hat{v}_{jk}(t)\big)\text{ log}\gamma_{jk}\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\);
\(\sum_{j=1}^{m} \sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{u}_{j}(t)\text{ log }p_j(y_t)\) with respect to the parameters of the state-dependent distributions.


The solution of this problem is:

Set \(\delta_{j} = \frac{\hat{u}_{j}(1)}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}}=\hat{u}_{j}(1)\)
Set \(\gamma_{jk} = f_{jk} \Big/ \sum_{k=1}^{m} f_{jk}\), where \(f_{jk} = \sum_{t=2}^{T} \hat v_{jk}(t)\)
The maximization of the third term depend on the structure of the state-dependent distributions.

The following code snippet is a naive implementation of the EM-algorithm applied to the example we have followed in this notebook

    C[t] = np.random.choice(states, p=Gamma[C[t-1]])
    Y[t] = np.random.normal(loc=mu[C[t]], scale=sigma[C[t]])

# Starting values for the EM
delta_hat = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
Gamma_hat = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]])
mu_hat = np.array([np.mean(Y) - np.std(Y), np.mean(Y) + np.std(Y)])
sigma_hat = np.array([np.std(Y), np.std(Y)])

tol = 1e-6

    v = delta_hat * P0
    w[0] = v.sum()
    alpha_hat[0] = v / w[0]

    for t in range(1, T):
        Pt = norm.pdf(Y[t], loc=mu_hat, scale=sigma_hat)
        v = (alpha_hat[t-1] @ Gamma_hat) * Pt
        w[t] = v.sum()
        alpha_hat[t] = v / w[t]

    log_L = np.log(w).sum()

    # Scaled backward
    beta_hat = np.zeros((T, m))
    beta_hat[T-1] = 1.0

    for t in range(T-2, -1, -1):
        Pt1 = norm.pdf(Y[t+1], loc=mu_hat, scale=sigma_hat)
        beta_hat[t] = (Gamma_hat @ (Pt1 * beta_hat[t+1])) / w[t+1]

    #  E-step
    u_hat = alpha_hat * beta_hat  

    v_hat = np.zeros((T, m, m))
    for t in range(1, T):
        Pt = norm.pdf(Y[t], loc=mu_hat, scale=sigma_hat)
        v_hat[t] = (alpha_hat[t-1][:, None] * Gamma_hat * Pt[None, :] * beta_hat[t][None, :]) / w[t]

    # M-step 
    delta_hat = u_hat[0].copy()

    f = v_hat[1:].sum(axis=0)

    peso = u_hat.sum(axis=0)  # total weight per state
    mu_hat = (u_hat * Y[:, None]).sum(axis=0) / peso
    sigma_hat = np.sqrt((u_hat * (Y[:, None] - mu_hat)**2).sum(axis=0) / peso)

    log_L_prev = log_L

title: Implementing Markov Chain Monte Carlo Algorithms for Multimodal Posterior Distributions
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms constitute the standard tool for exploring posterior distributions in Bayesian inference and their convergence guarantees are asymptotic. In finite runtime, however, a chain explores the region of the parameter space surrounding a starting point, and when the posterior is multimodal this typically means a single mode. Convergence is assessed through between-chain diagnostics which detect this only when the chains happen to have settled in different modes; otherwise the output looks unremarkable.
In hidden Markov models (HMMs) and Markov switching models (MSMs) multimodality arises from the likelihood itself because the states are exchangeable, so permuting the labels leaves the likelihood unchanged. Under an exchangeable prior the posterior inherits this symmetry, so the chain can then move between equivalent labellings, which makes state-specific posterior summaries meaningless. This problem is called label switching.
Even after correcting for label switching the posterior can remain multimodal with modes corresponding to different segmentations of the data rather than relabelling of the same one. Parallel tempering (PT) is a class of MCMC algorithms that addresses multimodality by running several chains along a sequence of tempered distributions and swapping states between them, improving the exploration between modes.
While PT is well developed theoretically, materials on implementing it are scarce. To reduce this gap, this repository documents a workflow for exploring multimodal posteriors with Stan, Pigeons.jl and emcee, using HMMs and MSMs as the working example. The notebooks cover how the algorithms work, common pitfalls and practical guidelines for people fitting these models.

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms constitute the standard tool for exploring posterior distributions in Bayesian inference and their convergence guarantees are asymptotic. In finite runtime, however, a chain explores the region of the parameter space surrounding a starting point, and when the posterior is multimodal this typically means a single mode. Convergence is assessed through between-chain diagnostics which detect this only when the chains happen to have settled in different modes; otherwise the output looks unremarkable.
In hidden Markov models (HMMs) and Markov switching models (MSMs) multimodality arises from the likelihood itself because the states are exchangeable, so permuting the labels leaves the likelihood unchanged. Under an exchangeable prior the posterior inherits this symmetry, so the chain can then move between equivalent labellings, which makes state-specific posterior summaries meaningless. This problem is called label switching.
Even after correcting for label switching the posterior can remain multimodal with modes corresponding to different segmentations of the data rather than relabelling of the same one. Parallel tempering (PT) is a class of MCMC algorithms that addresses multimodality by running several chains along a sequence of tempered distributions and swapping states between them, improving the exploration between modes.
While PT is well developed theoretically, materials on implementing it are scarce. To reduce this gap, this repository documents a workflow for exploring multimodal posteriors with Stan, Pigeons.jl and emcee, using HMMs and MSMs as the working example. The notebooks cover how the algorithms work, common pitfalls and practical guidelines for people fitting these models.

section: 2.1 Parameters and prior distributions of a Bayesian HMM
text:
2.1 Parameters and prior distributions of a Bayesian HMM
Recall that an HMM is a state-space model consisting of an observation process \(\{Y_t\}\) and an unobserved Markov process \(\{C_t\}\) taking values in a finite set of states \(\{1, \dots, m\}\) (Zucchini, MacDonald, and Langrock 2016). The realization of the observation process, \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \dots, y_T)\), is the data on which the posterior in Equation 1 is conditioned.
The parameters governing \(\{C_t\}\) are the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) and the transition probability matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), while each of the \(m\) state-dependent distributions, also known as emission distributions, has its own parameters \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_j\), \(j = 1, \dots, m\). We collect all of them in the parameter vector
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}, \boldsymbol{\eta}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\eta}_m),
\]
so that specifying a Bayesian HMM amounts to specifying a prior distribution \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) over each of these components.
Regarding the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) if it is stationary, then it can be derived from \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) so it leaves \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). In this notebook we make the assumption that the Markov process is homogeneous and stationary.

2.1.1 Transition probability matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\)
Each row of the transition probability matrix, \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i = (\gamma_{i1}, \dots, \gamma_{im})\) for \(i = 1, \dots, m\), is a vector of non-negative entries that sum to one. In other words, it belongs to the probability simplex
\[
\Delta^{m-1} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m : x_j \geq 0,\ \sum_{j=1}^{m} x_j = 1 \right\},
\]
the \((m-1)\)-dimensional set of all probability distributions over \(m\) elements (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004, 33). A natural choice for the prior for vectors in \(\Delta^{m-1}\) is the Dirichlet distribution, whose support is precisely this set (Frigyik, Kapila, and Gupta 2010). We therefore assume that the rows of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) are independent and that each follows a Dirichlet distribution,
\[
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i), \qquad \boldsymbol{\tau}_i = (\tau_{i1}, \dots, \tau_{im}), \quad \tau_{ij} > 0,
\]
with density
\[
p(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\tau}_i) = \frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i)} \prod_{j=1}^{m} \gamma_{ij}^{\tau_{ij} - 1},
\qquad
B(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i) = \frac{\prod_{j=1}^{m} \Gamma(\tau_{ij})}{\Gamma\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_{ij}\right)},
\tag{3}\]
where \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) denotes the gamma function and does not have to be confused with the transition probability matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\).
The concentration parameters \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i\) control the shape of this prior. They determine its mean, \(E[\gamma_{ij}] = \tau_{ij} / \tau_{i0}\) with \(\tau_{i0} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_{ij}\), and how concentrated it is around that mean: the larger \(\tau_{i0}\), the more informative the prior.
Following (Leos-Barajas and Michelot 2018) and (Gallegos-Herrada, Leos-Barajas, and Rosenthal 2026), we set \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i = \mathbf{1}_m\) for all rows. Besides its simplicity, this choice treats all states symmetrically, so the prior is invariant to a relabeling of the states; the consequences of this property are discussed in Section 3. Under this choice, Equation 3 reduces to
\[
p(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\tau}_i = \mathbf{1}_m) = \frac{\Gamma(m)}{\prod_{j=1}^{m} \Gamma(1)} \prod_{j=1}^{m} \gamma_{ij}^{0} = (m-1)!, \qquad \boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \in \Delta^{m-1}.
\tag{4}\]
Since this density does not depend on \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i\), the \(\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)\) prior is uniform on the simplex, with the constant \((m-1)!\) being the reciprocal of the volume of \(\Delta^{m-1}\). Uniformity on the simplex, however, does not imply uniformity on each entry: the marginal prior of each \(\gamma_{ij}\) is \(\text{Beta}(1, m-1)\), which places more mass near zero as \(m\) grows. In particular, it favors a priori low persistence in each state, i.e., small values of \(\gamma_{ii}\).


2.1.2 Initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\)
Since the entries of the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) must add to one and are all non-negative, it also has support on the probability simplex \(\Delta^{m-1}\).
We can treat \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) as a free parameter with its own prior distribution or to assume that the Markov process is stationary, so that \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is its stationary distribution.
Stationarity means that the chain is already in equilibrium when the observation process starts, so the distribution of the states does not change from one time point to the next (Zucchini, MacDonald, and Langrock 2016)
\[
\boldsymbol{\delta} \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \boldsymbol{\delta}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{m} \delta_j = 1.
\tag{5}\]
When the chain is irreducible, that is, when every state can be reached from any other state within a finite number of steps, the stationary distribution exists and is unique (Sargent and Stachurski 2022, Theorem 4.1.1).
Under the \(\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)\) prior of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), this condition holds with probability one: since the Dirichlet distribution is continuous on the simplex, no entry \(\gamma_{ij}\) is exactly zero with probability one, so every state can be reached from any other in a single step. The stationary distribution is then given by
\[
\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{1}_m \left( \mathbf{I}_m - \boldsymbol{\Gamma} + \mathbf{U} \right)^{-1},
\tag{6}\]
where \(\mathbf{1}_m\) is a row vector of ones, \(\mathbf{I}_m\) is the \(m \times m\) identity matrix and \(\mathbf{U}\) is the \(m \times m\) matrix of ones (Zucchini, MacDonald, and Langrock 2016). Under the stationarity assumption, \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is no longer a parameter but a deterministic function of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), so it requires no prior of its own: its prior distribution is the one induced by the prior on the rows of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\).
In this notebook we assume that the observation process starts when the chain is stationary and hence \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is the stationary distribution.


2.1.3 State-dependent distributions
Unlike the transition probabilities, the parameters of the state-dependent distributions do not share a common support, so there is no single prior that applies to every model. However, the choice can be guided by the support of each parameter. For example, real-valued parameters such as means call for priors on \(\mathbb{R}\), while positive parameters such as standard deviations or rates call for priors on \((0, \infty)\).
Another criterion for choosing priors is the algorithm used to draw samples from the posterior distribution. Gibbs samplers commonly rely on conjugate priors, which yield posterior conditional distributions in closed form given the hidden states. Stan, which we use later in this notebook, does not require conjugacy, so priors can be chosen for what they express rather than for their algebraic convenience.
When the state-dependent distributions are normal, the conjugate choice is a normal prior on each mean \(\mu_j\) and an inverse-gamma prior on each variance \(\sigma_j^2\) (Gelman et al. 2013). However, inverse-gamma priors with small parameters can be highly influential when a state has few observations, so weakly informative priors on the standard deviation, such as a half-normal or half-\(t\) distribution, are often preferred (Gelman 2006; Leos-Barajas and Michelot 2018). When the observations are counts modeled with a Poisson distribution in each state, a gamma prior on each rate \(\lambda_j\) is a natural choice, both because it is conjugate and because it has the appropriate support, although in Stan only the latter matters.
In this notebook we work with normal state-dependent distributions and use
\[
\mu_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, s_0^2), \qquad \sigma_j \sim \text{half-}\mathcal{N}(0, s_1^2), \qquad j = 1, \dots, m.
\tag{7}\]
Two features of these priors are important for what follows. First, the same prior is assigned to the parameters of every state, as was done for the rows of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), so that no state is distinguished a priori. The consequences of this choice are discussed in Section 2.3. Second, the priors are weakly informative rather than vague. In mixture models and HMMs, improper or nearly flat priors on the state-dependent parameters can lead to improper posterior distributions, since there is always a configuration in which some state is assigned no observations and the data provide no information about its parameters (Frühwirth-Schnatter 2006).

2.2 Likelihood via the forward algorithm
The last element needed to assemble the unnormalized posterior distribution is the likelihood. In the previous notebook we showed that, by summing over all possible sequences of hidden states, the likelihood of an HMM can be written as the matrix product
\[
L_T = \boldsymbol{\delta}\, \mathbf{P}(y_1)\, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\, \mathbf{P}(y_2) \cdots \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\, \mathbf{P}(y_T)\, \mathbf{1}_m^\top,
\tag{8}\]
where \(\mathbf{P}(y) = \text{diag}\big(p_1(y), \dots, p_m(y)\big)\) is the diagonal matrix of state-dependent densities evaluated at \(y\) (Zucchini, MacDonald, and Langrock 2016). In the notation of this notebook, \(L_T = L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})\), and under the stationarity assumption \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is the function of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) given in Equation 6. The forward algorithm evaluates Equation 8 at a cost that grows linearly in \(T\), instead of the \(m^T\) terms of the explicit sum over state sequences. In practice, the recursion is carried out on the log scale, since the product of \(T\) densities quickly underflows to zero (Leos-Barajas and Michelot 2018).
Assuming that the rows of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) and the parameters of each state are a priori independent, the log of the unnormalized posterior in Equation 2 becomes
\[
\log p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) = \log L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \mid \mathbf{1}_m) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \log p(\boldsymbol{\eta}_j) + \text{const.}
\tag{9}\]
No term for \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) appears, since under stationarity it carries no prior of its own. Each term of Equation 9 corresponds to one statement in the Stan program presented below.

text:
2.3 Exchangeable priors and posterior symmetry
In this section we show that relabeling the hidden states leaves the posterior unchanged. This follows from the likelihood being invariant to the labels and from the priors being exchangeable, that is, treating all states in the same way (Jasra, Holmes, and Stephens 2005). The resulting symmetry is what distinguishes the modes due to relabeling from genuinely different ones.
Consider an HMM with \(m\) states and label them state 1, state 2, …, state m. Note that this labeling from a mathematical perspective is irrelevant since the name state 1 initially assigned to a specific state can be assigned to any other state and the same goes to every other state. Under this situation, you can obtain \(m!\) different labelings.
Formally, each relabeling corresponds to a permutation \(\nu\) of the labels \(\{1, \dots, m\}\), and we denote by \(S_m\) the set of all \(m!\) such permutations (Jasra, Holmes, and Stephens 2005). Applying a permutation \(\nu \in S_m\) to the parameters of the HMM yields the relabeled parameter vector \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\), defined by
\[
\delta'_i = \delta_{\nu(i)}, \qquad \gamma'_{ij} = \gamma_{\nu(i)\nu(j)}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}'_j = \boldsymbol{\eta}_{\nu(j)}, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, m.
\tag{10}\]
where \(\nu \in S_{m}\) is the set of all \(m!\) permutations of \(1,2,...,m\).
For example, with \(m = 2\) there are two permutations, the identity, which leaves the labels unchanged, and \(\nu(1) = 2\), \(\nu(2) = 1\), which swaps them. Applying the latter to Equation 10 gives
\[
\boldsymbol{\delta}' = (\delta_2, \delta_1), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}' = \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_{22} & \gamma_{21} \\ \gamma_{12} & \gamma_{11} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
(\boldsymbol{\eta}'_1, \boldsymbol{\eta}'_2) = (\boldsymbol{\eta}_2, \boldsymbol{\eta}_1).
\]
Both parameter vectors describe exactly the same model, since the state previously called 2 is now called 1, together with its initial probability, its transition probabilities and its state-dependent parameters. Only the names have changed.
Note that relabeling the states does not change the likelihood. To see this, recall that Equation 8 is a compact form of the sum, over all possible \(m^T\) state sequences \((c_1, \dots, c_T)\), of the terms \(\delta_{c_1} p_{c_1}(y_1) \prod_{t=2}^{T} \gamma_{c_{t-1} c_t}\, p_{c_t}(y_t)\). By Equation 10, the term of the sequence \((c_1, \dots, c_T)\) evaluated at \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) equals the term of the sequence \((\nu(c_1), \dots, \nu(c_T))\) evaluated at \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). Since every sequence appears exactly once in the sum, relabeling only reorders its terms, and therefore \(L(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})\) for every \(\nu \in S_m\).
To see this, consider \(m=2\) states and \(T=2\) observations. In this case we have 4 possible sequences, so the likelihood is
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) =\; & \delta_1\, p_1(y_1)\, \gamma_{11}\, p_1(y_2) + \delta_1\, p_1(y_1)\, \gamma_{12}\, p_2(y_2) \\
+\; & \delta_2\, p_2(y_1)\, \gamma_{21}\, p_1(y_2) + \delta_2\, p_2(y_1)\, \gamma_{22}\, p_2(y_2),
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}\]
where the four terms correspond to the sequences \((1,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,1)\) and \((2,2)\). Now consider the permutation that swaps the labels, \(\nu(1) = 2\) and \(\nu(2) = 1\). By Equation 10, the term of the sequence \((1,2)\) evaluated at \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is
\[
\delta'_1\, p'_1(y_1)\, \gamma'_{12}\, p'_2(y_2) = \delta_2\, p_2(y_1)\, \gamma_{21}\, p_1(y_2),
\]
which is the term of the sequence \((2,1)\) in Equation 11.
In the same way, the terms of \((1,1)\), \((2,1)\) and \((2,2)\) evaluated at \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) equal the terms of \((2,2)\), \((1,2)\) and \((1,1)\) evaluated at \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). The four terms are therefore the same, only in a different order, and \(L(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})\). Thus, the likelihood is invariant to relabeling of the states.
The prior distribution is also invariant to relabeling, because it treats all states in the same way. Consider again \(m = 2\) and the permutation that swaps the labels. The rows of \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\) are exchanged and their entries reordered, but since the \(\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)\) prior is uniform on the simplex, every row receives the same density before and after the swap. The stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is computed from \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\), so its entries are swapped as well and no additional term appears.
A prior with this property, which assigns the same density to every relabeling of the parameters, is called exchangeable (Frühwirth-Schnatter 2001; Jasra, Holmes, and Stephens 2005).
Finally, the state-dependent parameters \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_2\) are exchanged, and since both states share the same prior, the product \(p(\boldsymbol{\eta}_1)\, p(\boldsymbol{\eta}_2)\) does not change. The same argument holds for any \(m\) and any permutation, so \(p(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) for every \(\nu \in S_m\). It is important to note, however, if we assign different priors to different states, for instance a prior centered at a low value for \(\mu_1\) and at a high value for \(\mu_2\), this invariance would no longer hold.
Since both the likelihood and the prior are invariant to relabeling, so is their product in Equation 2, and the posterior distribution satisfies
\[
p(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) \qquad \text{for every } \nu \in S_m.
\tag{12}\]
A posterior satisfying Equation 12 is said to be symmetric with respect to the labels, since every point \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) has \(m!\) counterparts \(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) with exactly the same posterior density.
Although relabeling leaves the posterior unchanged, it becomes problematic in practice when the posterior is explored with MCMC methods. By Equation 12, the marginal posterior distributions of the state-dependent parameters coincide across states, so that, for instance, \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) have the same marginal posterior. A sampler that has converged to this symmetric posterior therefore moves between the \(m!\) symmetric regions of high posterior density, and averages of state-specific quantities, such as the posterior mean of \(\mu_1\), become meaningless (Jasra, Holmes, and Stephens 2005; Papastamoulis 2016). This phenomenon is known as label switching and methods for alleviating this phenomenon are discussed in Section 3.

3.1 Ordering constraints
Jasra, Holmes, and Stephens (2005) and Leos-Barajas and Michelot (2018) suggest imposing constraints on the parameters can improve inference on the parameters. A natural choice is to order one parameter of the state-dependent distributions, for example the means, \(\mu_1 < \mu_2 < \cdots < \mu_m\). Under this constraint, only one of the \(m!\) copies of the posterior remains.
This approach works well when the marginal posteriors of the ordered parameters, within a single copy, do not overlap. When they do overlap, the constraint truncates the posterior and biases the estimates, because the boundary \(\mu_j = \mu_{j+1}\) cuts through regions of high posterior density.
Using the example exposed in Section 2.4, we can impose restrictions on the means \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\). This is achived in Stan by replacing the definition of mu in the block parameters.
// parameters
parameters{
    ordered[m] mu; // means of state dependent distributions (now is a ordered array)
    
    // Rest of the code    
}
We have a Stan program with the ordering constraint stored in stan/02_ex1_normal_order.stan. We compile it and fit it to the same data with the same settings as before. Unlike the unconstrained fit, all \(\hat{R}\) values are now close to one, so we have convergence. The posterior means of \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are \(-2.10\) and \(1.92\), close to the true values of \(-2\) and \(2\).
The constraint works well in this example because the marginal posteriors of \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) do not overlap. The 95th percentile of \(\mu_1\) is \(-1.99\), well below the 5th percentile of \(\mu_2\), which is \(1.77\). The boundary \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\) therefore lies in a region with no posterior mass.

# Compile the Stan program
model_ord = CmdStanModel(stan_file="../stan/02_ex1_normal_order.stan")

# Fit the model 
fit_ord = model_ord.sample(data=stan_data, chains=8, parallel_chains=8, seed=123)

# Fit Summary
fit_ord.summary()

title: Bayesian Hidden Markov Models and the label switching problem
text:
3.2 Post-hoc relabelling
Relabelling algorithms are a class of methods for dealing with label switching that rely on Bayesian decision theory (Stephens 2000; Jasra, Holmes, and Stephens 2005). Summarizing the posterior, for example by reporting a point estimate of the state-specific parameters, can be seen as choosing an action \(a\) from a set of possible actions \(\mathcal{A}\). This summary, called an action \(a\) can be a point estimate of the stet-specific parameters (such as \(\mu_j\) or \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\)) or the probabilities \(P(C_t = j| \mathbf{y})\) of each state at time \(t\). Each cpice of action comes weith a loss function \(\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{A} \times\boldsymbol{\theta}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) that measures how far \(a\) is from the parameters, and the best acttion is the one that minimizes the posterior expected loss (Stephens 2000).
For this, suppose that there is a function \(\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{A} \times\boldsymbol{\theta}\rightarrow[0, \infty]\)n such that
\[
L(a,\boldsymbol{\theta})=\underset{\nu \in S_{m}}{\text{min}}{\{L_{0}(a, \nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\}}
\]
That is, \(L(a,\boldsymbol{\theta})\) measures the loss with respect to the relabelling of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) that is closest to \(a\). As a result, \(L\) is invariant to permutations of the labels, since \(L(a, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = L(a, \nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\) for every \(\nu \in S_m\).
In practice, we have samples of the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(2)}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(N)}\) from a particular chain, that we assume is stationary. One way to compute the expected posterior loss is by Monte Carlo
\[
\mathbb{E}(L(a,\boldsymbol{\theta})) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \min_{\nu_t} \left[ L_0\{a;\, \nu_t(\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)})\} \right]
= \min_{\nu_1, \dots, \nu_N} \left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} L_0\{a;\, \nu_t(\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)})\} \right]
\tag{17}\]
